content: 1. Pravastatin was neither embryolethal nor teratogenic in rats at doses up to 1000 mg/kg daily or in rabbits at doses up to 50 mg/kg daily. 2. In pregnant rats administered oral gavage doses of 4, 20, 100, 500, and 1000 mg/kg/day from gestation days 7 through 17 (organogenesis period), increased offspring mortality and skeletal anomalies were observed at 100 mg/kg/day. 3. In pregnant rats given oral gavage doses of 10, 100, and 1000 mg/kg/day from gestation day 17 through lactation day 21 (weaning period), increased offspring mortality and developmental delays were observed at 100 mg/kg/day. 4. There is no guidance from the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) regarding the use of pravastatin in pregnant women. 5. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of pravastatin during labor and delivery. 6. A small amount of pravastatin is excreted in human breast milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, women taking pravastatin should not breastfeed. 7. Pravastatin crosses the placenta and is found in fetal tissue at 30% of maternal plasma levels following a single 20 mg/kg dose administered to pregnant rats on gestation day 18. 8. Studies in lactating rats indicate that pravastatin is secreted into breast milk at levels 0.2 to 6. 9. The safety and effectiveness of pravastatin in children and adolescents aged 8 to 18 years have been evaluated in a 2-year placebo-controlled study. Adverse experiences in pravastatin-treated patients were generally similar to those in placebo-treated patients, with influenza and headache commonly reported in both groups. Doses greater than 40 mg have not been studied in this population. 10. Female children and adolescents of childbearing potential should be counseled on appropriate contraceptive methods while on pravastatin therapy. 11. Double-blind, placebo-controlled studies of pravastatin in children under 8 years of age have not been conducted. 12. In geriatric use, two secondary prevention trials (CARE and LIPID) included 6593 subjects treated with pravastatin 40 mg for up to 6 years. Of these, 36.1% were aged 65 and older, and 0.8% were aged 75 and older. The beneficial effects of pravastatin in reducing cardiovascular events and modifying lipid profiles in elderly subjects were similar to those observed in younger subjects. The adverse event profile in the elderly was also similar to that in the overall population. No differences in responses to pravastatin between elderly and younger patients have been identified. 13. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of pravastatin with respect to specific gender or racial populations. 14. There is no FDA guidance on the use of pravastatin in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 15. There is no FDA guidance on the use of pravastatin in women of reproductive potential or in males. 16. There is no FDA guidance on the use of pravastatin in immunocompromised patients. 17. Pravastatin is administered orally. The FDA package insert contains no information regarding drug monitoring or IV compatibility. 18. Limited experience exists with pravastatin overdose. 19. Pravastatin is a reversible inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early and rate-limiting step in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway. Pravastatin also reduces VLDL and triglycerides while increasing HDL-C. 20. Pravastatin sodium is a member of the statin class of lipid-lowering compounds, which competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. It is chemically designated as 1-Naphthalene-heptanoic acid, 1,2,6,7,8,8a-hexahydro-β,δ,6-trihydroxy-2-methyl-8-(2-methyl-1-oxobutoxy)-, monosodium salt. It is an odorless, white to off-white, fine or crystalline powder, relatively polar and hydrophilic, with a partition coefficient (octanol/water) of 0.59 at pH 7.0. It is soluble in methanol and water (>300 mg/mL), slightly soluble in isopropanol, and practically insoluble in acetone, acetonitrile, chloroform, and ether. 21. Pravastatin is available for oral administration as 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, and 80 mg tablets. Inactive ingredients include croscarmellose sodium, lactose, magnesium oxide, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, and povidone. The 10 mg tablet also contains red ferric oxide, the 20 mg and 80 mg tablets contain yellow ferric oxide, and the 40 mg tablet contains a green lake blend (a mixture of D&C Yellow No. 10-Aluminum Lake and FD&C Blue No. 1-Aluminum Lake). 22. The FDA package insert for pravastatin contains no information regarding pharmacodynamics. 23. Pravastatin is administered orally in its active form. In human studies, peak plasma concentrations occur 1 to 1.5 hours after oral administration. The average oral absorption of pravastatin is 34%, and its absolute bioavailability is 17%, based on urinary recovery of total radiolabeled drug. Food reduces systemic bioavailability, but the lipid-lowering effects are similar whether the drug is taken with food or 1 hour before meals. 24. Pravastatin plasma concentrations, including area under the concentration-time curve (AUC), Cmax, and steady-state minimum (Cmin), are directly proportional to the administered dose. Systemic bioavailability of pravastatin following a bedtime dose is decreased by 60% compared to a morning dose. Despite this decrease, the efficacy of pravastatin administered once daily in the evening was marginally more effective than that after a morning dose, although not statistically significant. The coefficient of variation (CV) for AUC, based on between-subject variability, was 50% to 60%. The geometric means of pravastatin Cmax and AUC following a 20 mg dose in the fasted state were 26.5 ng/mL and 59.8 ng·hr/mL, respectively.
